hook: The monk whose pea plants revealed the laws of heredity, ignored until after his death.

pages.x: Johann Mendel was born in 1822 in Heinzendorf, a village in Austrian Silesia, now in the Czech Republic. His parents were poor farmers, and as a boy he tended the orchard and kept bees. His family struggled to pay for his schooling.
To be able to keep studying, in 1843 he became a monk at the Abbey of St Thomas in Brno, and took the name Gregor. The abbey was a centre of learning, with a library, scientists, and a garden.
The abbey sent him to the University of Vienna to study science. Twice he failed the exam to become a qualified teacher, so for years he taught as a substitute.

From 1856 to 1863, in the abbey garden, he grew and cross-bred some 28,000 pea plants, counting tall and short, smooth and wrinkled, green and yellow. Traits passed on in neat ratios, such as 3 to 1, and some skipped a generation.
pages.fx: He had found that traits are passed on in separate units, one from each parent: what we now call genes.

pages.x: He presented his results in 1865 and published them the next year. Almost no one understood them. A famous botanist told him to try hawkweed instead, a plant whose odd way of breeding made his laws seem not to work.

In 1868 he was elected abbot, and had little time left for science, though he still kept bees and recorded the weather every day. He is said to have told a friend: "My time will come." He died in 1884, and his papers were burned.
In 1900, three scientists working separately found the same laws, then came across his paper. Sixteen years after his death, Mendel was hailed as the father of genetics.
Mendel found the basic laws of heredity, how traits pass from parents to children. DNA tests, new crops and the study of inherited diseases all build on his peas.
pts: Ignored until 16 years after his death
